newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche may monitor MGAM business from Frankfurt.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche may monitor MGAM business from Frankfurt.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG said on Tuesday its decision to send a German manager to Morgan Grenfell was linked to a possible rerouting of management reporting lines for its UK unit trust business to Frankfurt.

A spokesman said that while Deutsche had for several years been considering putting its UK trust business under supervision from Frankfurt, the recent problems at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) had given these thoughts new impetus.
But he stressed that Deutsche was considering shifting reporting lines, not the management of funds themselves.

MGAM last week temporarily suspended trading in three of its European funds due to suspected irregularities in an affair which has embarrassed Deutsche and rattled confidence in unit trusts, hitherto seen as a safe home for an investor.
"For several years we have been thinking about managing the fund business for private clients from Frankfurt," Deutsche spokesman Hellmut Hartmann told Reuters.
"After the problems in London these considerations have been renewed and it could well be that this will happen but no decision has been taken yet.
"In this context we have sent one of our fund managers to London to act as an adviser for measures being taken there."
Management supervision for Morgan Grenfell's institutional fund business would remain in London, Hartmann said.
Analysts said a switch of management responsibility from London to Frankfurt would be a logical consequence of Deutsche's reorganisation announced in July.

Under that revamp, Deutsche created a division called Private Customers, run by board members Georg Krupp and Tessin von Heydebreck, which included private asset management. But Morgan Grenfell's unit trust business remained allocated to a separate division, Investment Banking. That may now change.

The manager of two of the troubled unit trusts, Peter Young, has been suspended and his assets frozen pending a probe into the management of the funds, which held a high proportion of speculative, unlisted, high-technology stocks.
Deutsche last week took the irregular stocks onto its books in return for a 180 million pounds ($279.7 million) cash injection into MGAM.
It appointed Udo Behrenwaldt, a managing director of its German investment subsidiary DWS Deutsche Gesellschaft fuer Wertpapiersparen mbH, as an adviser to MGAM in London.

That was the first step towards stricter management supervision from Frankfurt after Deutsche's head of global fund management, Rolf Breuer, last week announced an overhaul of internal controls at MGAM.
The bank said Behrenwaldt had temporarily taken on a consultative role and would not take part in active management. Behrenwaldt is in charge of DWS' global equity fund business.

Meanwhile, Hartmann reiterated that Deutsche Morgan Grenfell would pay compensation if the current investigation by the British fund industry watchdog, the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO), found that it was liable.

"If the results should show that due to IMRO regulations or other applicable legal requirements a compensation is due, Morgan Grenfell will of course have to pay it, that is self-evident" Hartmann said.
Analysts said the affair was likely to hurt MGAM's 1996 earnings as well as its image.
"The main problem is that this is another illustration of them being asleep on the watch," said Bryan Crossley, banking analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett in London.

Konrad Becker, an analyst at Merck, Finck in Frankfurt, said he had lowered his 1996 earnings-per-share forecast for Deutsche to 4.50 marks from five marks to account for the cash injection and possible compensation payments.
But Becker said he was maintaining his buy recommendation because of Deutsche's sound strategy in expanding its investment banking.
"Their development won't suffer in the long term provided they tighten controls appreciably and so regain investor confidence," Becker said.
